question: What is a 'vessel not under command' under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: Any vessel without a licensed operator aboard
choice_b: A vessel that has simply run out of fuel but can still be steered normally
choice_c: A vessel operating without current registration
choice_d: A vessel which, through some exceptional circumstance, is unable to maneuver as required by the Rules and is therefore unable to keep out of the way of another vessel
explanation: A vessel not under command is one that, through some exceptional circumstance such as mechanical failure, is unable to maneuver as the Rules require and therefore cannot keep out of the way of other vessels.

question: Which of the following is an example of a 'vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver' under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: A vessel engaged in laying, servicing, or picking up a submarine cable, or engaged in dredging operations, where the nature of the work restricts its ability to keep out of the way of other vessels
choice_b: A vessel simply traveling at a slow, no-wake speed
choice_c: A small sailboat that is temporarily becalmed with no wind
choice_d: A vessel towing a single water skier on a calm lake
explanation: A vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver is one that, by the nature of her work (such as cable laying, dredging, or similar operations), cannot deviate from her course as needed to keep clear of another vessel.

question: Under the Navigation Rules' definitions, which of these does NOT count as a vessel 'engaged in fishing' entitled to that special right-of-way status?
choice_a: A vessel actively working a large trawl net that limits its ability to turn
choice_b: A vessel trolling with a single fishing line while underway, since trolling lines do not restrict the vessel's maneuverability
choice_c: A commercial vessel with long-lines deployed that restrict its course changes
choice_d: A vessel whose nets are actively restricting its ability to maneuver
explanation: The Rules define 'engaged in fishing' as using nets, lines, trawls, or other apparatus that restricts maneuverability -- but specifically excludes fishing with trolling lines, since trolling does not restrict maneuverability.

question: In a narrow channel or fairway, where should a vessel keep, as far as is safe and practicable?
choice_a: In the exact center of the channel at all times
choice_b: As near the outer limit on her own port side as possible
choice_c: As near the outer limit of the channel that lies on her own starboard side as is safe and practicable
choice_d: Wherever is most convenient, with no preferred side specified
explanation: A vessel proceeding along a narrow channel or fairway must keep as near the outer limit of the channel on her starboard side as is safe and practicable.

question: In a narrow channel, what is required of a vessel less than 20 meters long or a sailing vessel with respect to vessels that can navigate safely only within that channel?
choice_a: It automatically has the right-of-way over any larger vessel in the channel
choice_b: It must anchor and wait until the larger vessel has completely left the area
choice_c: It must cross directly ahead of the larger vessel as quickly as possible
choice_d: It must not impede the safe passage of a vessel that can navigate safely only within the narrow channel or fairway
explanation: A vessel of less than 20 meters or a sailing vessel must not impede the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only within a narrow channel or fairway.

question: May a vessel cross a narrow channel if doing so would impede the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only within that channel?
choice_a: No -- a vessel must not cross a narrow channel or fairway if crossing would impede the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only within that channel
choice_b: Yes, crossing traffic always has right-of-way over vessels following the channel
choice_c: Yes, as long as the crossing vessel sounds one short blast beforehand
choice_d: The Navigation Rules do not address crossing a narrow channel
explanation: A vessel must not cross a narrow channel or fairway if doing so would impede the passage of a vessel that can navigate safely only within that channel.

question: In a narrow channel, is a vessel engaged in fishing permitted to impede the passage of other vessels navigating within the channel?
choice_a: Yes, fishing vessels always have absolute priority in narrow channels
choice_b: No -- a vessel engaged in fishing must not impede the passage of any other vessel navigating within a narrow channel or fairway
choice_c: Only sailing vessels are restricted from impeding traffic in narrow channels, not fishing vessels
choice_d: Fishing vessels may anchor anywhere in a narrow channel without restriction
explanation: A vessel engaged in fishing must not impede the passage of any other vessel navigating within a narrow channel or fairway.

question: As the stand-on vessel, at what point may you first take action to avoid a collision, rather than continuing to hold course and speed?
choice_a: Only after physical contact between the vessels has already occurred
choice_b: You may never deviate from your course and speed under any circumstance
choice_c: As soon as it becomes apparent to you that the give-way vessel is not taking the appropriate action required of her
choice_d: Immediately upon sighting any other vessel, regardless of what that vessel is doing
explanation: The stand-on vessel must initially keep her course and speed, but may take action to avoid collision as soon as it becomes apparent that the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.17, Rule 17 - Action by Stand-On Vessel

question: If the give-way vessel fails to act and a collision can no longer be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone, what must the stand-on vessel do?
choice_a: Continue to hold course and speed no matter what, since she is not at fault
choice_b: Immediately reverse engines and come to a complete stop regardless of circumstances
choice_c: Sound the danger signal and take no further action of her own
choice_d: Take whatever action will best help to avoid the collision
explanation: If a collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone, the stand-on vessel must take whatever action will best aid in avoiding the collision.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.17, Rule 17 - Action by Stand-On Vessel

question: When a power-driven stand-on vessel takes action to avoid a collision with a vessel approaching from ahead, what maneuver should she avoid if circumstances permit?
choice_a: Altering course to port for a vessel that is on her own port side
explanation: A power-driven stand-on vessel taking action under this rule should, if circumstances allow, avoid altering course to port for a vessel on her own port side.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.17, Rule 17 - Action by Stand-On Vessel

question: Under the Rule 18 hierarchy of responsibility, must a vessel engaged in fishing keep out of the way of a vessel not under command or a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver?
choice_a: No -- a fishing vessel outranks every other type of vessel without exception
choice_b: Yes -- a vessel engaged in fishing must keep out of the way of a vessel not under command and a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver
choice_c: Only if the fishing vessel happens to be anchored at the time
choice_d: The Navigation Rules do not rank fishing vessels against any other vessel type
explanation: A vessel engaged in fishing, while she has priority over sailing and power-driven vessels, must still keep out of the way of a vessel not under command and a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver.

question: Besides vessels not under command and vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver, what other type of vessel must a sailing vessel underway also keep out of the way of?
choice_a: Any power-driven vessel that happens to be faster
choice_b: A personal watercraft of any kind
choice_d: No other vessel -- a sailboat under sail is always the stand-on vessel against every other type of vessel
explanation: A sailing vessel underway must keep out of the way of a vessel not under command, a vessel restricted in her ability to maneuver, and a vessel engaged in fishing -- a sailboat is not automatically stand-on against fishing vessels.

question: The Navigation Rules for conduct in restricted visibility apply specifically to what situation, unlike the ordinary meeting, crossing, and overtaking rules?
choice_a: Only vessels that are at anchor
choice_b: Only power-driven vessels longer than 65 feet
choice_c: Any two vessels that can plainly see one another, regardless of weather
choice_d: Vessels that are not in sight of one another, navigating in or near an area of restricted visibility such as fog
explanation: The restricted visibility rule governs vessels not in sight of one another navigating in or near an area of restricted visibility, distinct from the meeting, crossing, and overtaking rules, which apply when vessels are in sight of each other.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.19, Rule 19 - Conduct of Vessels in Restricted Visibility

question: In restricted visibility such as fog, what speed must every vessel proceed at, and what must a power-driven vessel keep ready?
choice_a: A safe speed adapted to the prevailing circumstances and conditions, with her engines ready for immediate maneuvering
choice_b: Full cruising speed, in order to clear the area of reduced visibility as quickly as possible
choice_c: A fixed speed of 5 mph regardless of vessel size, traffic, or conditions
choice_d: There is no speed requirement in restricted visibility, only a lookout requirement
explanation: In restricted visibility every vessel must proceed at a safe speed adapted to the prevailing circumstances and conditions, and a power-driven vessel must have her engines ready for immediate maneuver.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.19, Rule 19 - Conduct of Vessels in Restricted Visibility

question: If you detect another vessel by radar alone in restricted visibility and determine a close-quarters situation is developing with a vessel forward of your beam, which action should generally be avoided if circumstances allow?
choice_b: Altering course to port for a vessel forward of the beam, other than one being overtaken
choice_d: Continuing to monitor the situation by radar
explanation: When action is taken to avoid a close-quarters situation with a vessel detected by radar forward of the beam, an alteration of course to port should generally be avoided, other than for a vessel being overtaken.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.19, Rule 19 - Conduct of Vessels in Restricted Visibility

question: In restricted visibility, upon hearing what appears to be the fog signal of another vessel forward of your beam, what must you do?
choice_a: Increase speed to clear the area where the signal was heard as quickly as possible
choice_b: Ignore the signal unless the other vessel becomes visible
choice_c: Reduce speed to the minimum at which you can be kept on her course, taking all way off if necessary, and navigate with extreme caution until the danger of collision is over
choice_d: Sound five short blasts and continue to hold course and speed
explanation: On hearing a fog signal apparently forward of the beam, a vessel must reduce speed to the minimum at which she can be kept on course, taking all way off if necessary, and navigate with extreme caution until the danger of collision is over.
source_note: 33 CFR 83.19, Rule 19 - Conduct of Vessels in Restricted Visibility
